questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Personal connection to the destination (heritage / friends there/ etc.)

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Opportunities to do experimental work in my field and wanting to visit my friends in Japan.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: When you arrive at the university you are given a envelope full of brochures, guides, important passwords and documents that need to be filled out before various deadlines - which was practical, but a bit overwhelming.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer:
A japanese student from my lab helped me go to the ward office to register my address and fill out insurance forms etc. 
And as mentioned above, I was given an envelope with all the important paper work I needed to do.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: Staff and students are very happy to help you out when you don't understand the paperwork or can't read the kanji - just reach out!

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: Initially I was staying at a cheap Airbnb in the center of Osaka (which there are a ton of), but since the commute was very long I ended up moving into the Toyonaka International House, which was very nice! Cheap rent (around 1600 DKK a month), right on the campus and nice facilities. There is also a less popular dorm at Toyonaka campus, but that one is only for men and is (and here I quote a guy from my lab who lived there for a month) "So full of cockroaches it is impossible to live in." - so you should probably avoid that one.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: Each room has a kitchen stove with one gas burner, a kitchen counter, a fridge, a small freezer and a sink. Also there's a larger shared kitchen in the A building which has an oven.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: Although there are no kitchen utensils in the rooms, the Toyonaka International House has an area in the lounge where people leave stuff they no longer need when they move out. Here you can probably find most of what you need without having to go out and buy it - I found plates, cutlery, pans, mugs and even an electric kettle!

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I recommend participating in the events arranged by the dorm to make friends and learn about japanese culture! There are a ton of events all year round - ranging from ikebana lessons to halloween parties and onigiri workshops.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Acquiring all the necessary documents was a bureaucratic hell - although perhaps some of that was due to the extra documents required because of corona (for the visa application).

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You need a ton of stuff like a health certificate from a doctor, relevant classes, grades, future aspirations, letter of recommendation, fields of interest, the actual application, language score (TOEFL or JLPT) etc. The process of acquiring these things is pretty time consuming - so start as early as you can!

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: You're given a very detailed guide for how to apply and what documents you will need. And you can always email the Osaka Univ. Student Exchange for help or clarification if you need it - they usually answer within a day!

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Since I registered to FrontierLab I only had to find a laboratory I wanted to do research in - which I managed.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: The laboratory work is very time consuming. So although they also offer Japanese courses, I would advise against taking these if you want to focus on your project.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I took the FrontierLab program which does not have a formal level.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Learning to work in a laboratory is probably very similar across universities. Although I wouldn't know what it's like to learn that at UCPH since corona cancelled all of my lab exercises :(

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: FrontierLab (D)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: FrontierLab! And no additional courses unless you want to stress yourself out.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Insurances! Even though you have a travel insurance from Denmark, you are still required to buy a lot of insurances in Japan.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Eating out is very cheap!

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Especially at Toyonaka campus there are a ton of different clubs that you can join - basketball, dance ice hockey, guitar, the ojousama club (?), the Love Live! research club (??), juggling club, the traditional japanese comedy club, lego club, bands, vegetarian club, coffee club - the list goes on. Although joining these clubs without knowing any japanese would maybe be difficult.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There are some different organizations that plan monthly events especially for international students at Osaka University. Information about these is included in the envelope with documents you get when you arrive.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: There's a facebook group called "Outdoor Adventure Team OGURA" which you should definitely try to join if you like hiking and nature! I think you can only join by being invited by an existing member, but most indian and indonesian students are members, so just talk to one of them! It's run by a professor (Ogura) who apparently has too much money, because he often pays for large parts of the trips out of his own pocket - which means you can go on really spectacular trips all across Japan for super cheap (like 1000 yen). I went on one day trips to Ise, Mt. Seppiko and Soni Kogen and on a 3-day snow hike in Shirakawago. Highly recommend!

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Visit Nara and Kyoto!

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: I speak japanese and have lived in Japan before, so for me it was very easy.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer:
Join events and activities! That's where you'll meet the other international students. And if you speak japanese I don't need to give you any tips - japanese people will love talking to you.
Oh, and participate in all the nomikai in your lab even if you don't speak japanese.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The hardest part to adjust to was the japanese work culture - I usually went to the lab from 9-18 and I was often the last to be there and the first to go home...

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The food!!! And having a bath tub even though I lived in a dorm room.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1) If all the deadlines and rules seem impossible remember that people are people and you can usually talk to someone to figure it out
2) Join Prof. Oguras outdoor adventure club
3) Eat lots of ramen

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Bring a bicycle helmet! Bikes are easy to rent or buy in Japan, but helmets are not.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Learning to work in a lab and getting to know new people.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The application process and the paperwork after you arrive.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Have fun!!!

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
